claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is primarily governed by sluggish diffusion.
High configurational entropy and associated lattice distortions hinder atomic mobility and phase segregation.
The initial high-entropy nanoalloys are uniform and single-phase, with equiatomic or near-equiatomic elemental distributions.
High-entropy nanoalloys possess local lattice distortions and highly heterogeneous atomic-scale chemical environments.
High configurational entropy in multielement systems creates complex local chemical environments.
High configurational entropy in multielement systems creates substantial lattice strain.
Complex local environments and lattice strain raise atomic diffusion barriers.
Raised diffusion barriers produce inherently sluggish diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion delays atomic rearrangement and phase segregation at high temperatures.
Under high-temperature exposure, high-entropy nanoalloys will retain a more uniform, single-phase structure than binary or lower-entropy alloys.
High-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less grain growth than binary or lower-entropy alloys under comparable high-temperature conditions.
High-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less elemental segregation than binary or lower-entropy alloys under comparable high-temperature conditions.
Binary or lower-entropy alloys undergo faster phase separation and coarsening than high-entropy nanoalloys.
The proposed stability effect may diminish at temperatures significantly above 1200 degrees Celsius because thermal energy can surpass diffusion activation barriers.
Strong chemical affinities between constituent elements can force phase separation and override the proposed sluggish-diffusion stabilization.
The temperature threshold and magnitude of sluggish-diffusion effects vary with elemental combination and nanoscale features.
